Items.Authors: Toshiyuki Mizuki, Justin Hom, Bertrand Mennesson, Ramya Anche, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Vanessa P. Bailey, Koji Kawabata, Mitsuhiko Takeuchi, Motohide Tamura, Naoshi Murakami, John Livingston, Jason J. Wang, Schuyler G. Wolff, Guillermo Gonzalez, Eric Shen, Tsutsumi Nagai, Taichi Uyajma
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph community participation program: calibration strategy for the Mueller matrix using on-sky sources
Items.Abstract: The Coronagraphic Instrument on the Roman Space Telescope has a visible polarimetric mode. Accurate calibration of its polarization response is essential for characterizing debris disks, detecting planetary polarization, and diagnosing polarization aberrations. We will observe two unpolarized standards and two polarized standards with intrinsic polarization angles separated by about 45 degrees. These four stars provide the necessary constraints to solve the Mueller matrix such that the known polarization degrees and angles of the standards are correctly recovered. Standards must be single, bright enough for high S/N without saturating, and sufficiently polarized; visibility and operational constraints also apply. From optical catalogs we identified 72 candidates and began a precursor campaign targeting 21 northern objects. Multi-band HONIR polarimetry on the Kanata 1.5 m telescope measures wavelength dependence and enables Serkowski-law extrapolation to the Roman filters.

Items.Authors: Jingwen Zhang, Sophie Noiret, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Jason Wang, Neil Zimmerman, Eric Shen, Alexis Lau, Elodie Choquet, Taichi Uyajma, Chen Xie, Jessica Gersh-Range, Julien Girard, Vanessa Bailey, John Krist, Kevin Ludwick, Alexis Bidot, Arthur Vigan
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph community participation program: corgisim, a simulation suite for the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Coronagraphic Instrument
Items.Abstract: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope will feature a pathfinder Coronagraph Instrument to demonstrate advanced high-contrast imaging from space. Roman Coronagraph could obtain imaging and spectroscopy of Jupiter analogs in reflected visible light for the first time. We present the work of developing an open-source simulation package “corgisim” as part of the Roman Coronagraph Community Participate Program. Built on established optical propagation libraries such as PROPER and CGISim, corgisim provides a publicly available Python framework for end-to-end simulations of Roman-CGI observations. The package produces high-fidelity, format-compliant data for pre-launch calibration, pipeline testing, and community applications such as target planning and selection and observation planning. We will give an overview of corgisim’s infrastructure, and current implementation across planned imaging, polarimetry, and spectroscopy modes. We will also provide guidance on how users can employ the software.

Items.Authors: Amanda Chavez, Jason Wang, Vanessa Bailey, Maxwell Millar-Blanchaer, Julien H. Girard, Sergi Hildebrandt, John Krist, Julia Milton, Marie Ygouf
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: data reduction pipeline astrometric calibration
Items.Abstract: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program has led the development of a python-based, open source data reduction pipeline (corgidrp) to quantify the performance of the Roman Space Telescope coronagraph instrument and to process its data products. Here, we present the astrometric calibration function within the greater data reduction pipeline, outline the methods for computing critical astrometric calibration measurements, and contextualize this calibration process within corgidrp. Additionally, we discuss the results of end-to-end testing and show that all formal Technology Demonstration Threshold Requirements for this calibration step are satisfied.

Items.Authors: Ramya M. Anche, Toshiyuki Mizuki, Vanessa P. Bailey, Eric J. Cady, Clarissa Do Ó, Jessica A. Gersh-Range, Justin Hom, Alexis Lau, John Livingston, Bertrand Mennesson, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Julia Milton, Naoshi Murakami, Tsutsumi Nagai, Sophie Noiret, Eric Shen, Motohide Tamura, Taichi Uyajma, Jason J. Wang, Schuyler G. Wolff, Cynthia Wong, Chen Xie, Marie Ygouf, Jingwen Zhang, Julien H. Girard
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: simulation of on-sky polarimetric observations, data reduction, and analysis
Items.Abstract: Reflected-light polarimetry of an exoplanet helps constrain and break degeneracies in atmospheric properties, and polarized light observations of debris disks enable exploration of the disk’s dust-grain properties. The best-effort polarimetric mode of the Roman Coronagraph Instrument will be able to perform multi-wavelength observations of planetary systems using the Hybrid Lyot Coronagraph (HLC) and the Shaped Pupil Coronagraph (SPC). In this paper, we demonstrate the capabilities of the polarimetric mode of the Roman Coronagraph for targets chosen in the nominal observing plan. We simulate science target observations and calibration products using the corgisim package and perform data reduction and analysis using the corgidrp, incorporating all noise factors and instrumental polarization effects from modeled Mueller matrices. The final retrieved polarization fraction (p) indicates that the polarimetry mode of the Roman Coronagraph Instrument meets the goal uncertainty of ~ 3%.

Items.Authors: Dmitry Savransky, Rifah Tasnim, Saanika Choudhary, Hovik Grigoryan, Justin Hom, Bijan Nemati, Neil Zimmerman, Ramya Anche, Nicholas Phillips, Louie Donesa, Parth Mittal, Amira Razack, Savaas Iqbal, Javier Majumdar, Schuyler G. Wolff, Vanessa P. Bailey
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: target database and tools
Items.Abstract: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope’s Coronagraph Instrument will, for the first time, demonstrate high-contrast imaging with active wavefront control in visible wavelengths from space. In preparation for the Coronagraph’s commissioning and observing programs, the Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program has developed a target database and associated ecosystem of publicly accessible tools for observation planning and scheduling. The target database includes planet and disk hosts, calibration stars, reference stars, and engineering program targets. The database is designed to operate in conjunction with a variety of tools, including an exposure time calculator, a pointing and keepout calculator, and a reference star selection tool. We describe the current schema and contents of the database and demonstrate how it and its associated tools are being used for observation planning.

Items.Authors: Arthur Vigan, Alexis Bidot, Vincent Chambouleyron, Garreth Ruane, Laurent Pueyo, Mamadou N'Diaye, Kjetil Dohlen
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: using the Zernike wavefront sensor for a full characterisation of the Roman Space Telescope and the Coronagraph Instrument
Items.Abstract: The Roman Space Telescope Coronagraph Instrument (CGI) will demonstrate a series of technologies and techniques to enable the direct detection of reflected-light planets with space-based observatories. Among the several available observing modes and coronagraphic devices embarked in CGI, there is a transmissive Zernike wavefront sensor (ZWFS) that can be used to directly measure optical aberrations in the system. In this work, we advocate for the commissioning of this unique observing mode. We investigate the sensitivity of the ZWFS and demonstrate how it can be used for a full observatory characterisation. We use the CGI simulator and other tools developed and supported by the Roman community participation program (CPP). This type of analysis is crucial for understanding the stability of the Roman observatory and to prepare the path towards HWO.

Items.Authors: D. Gale, C. Salas-Matamoros, M. Velázquez, W. Mejías, G. Lara, A. Fallas, F. Ruíz, Ó. Núñez, E. Ibarra
Items.Title: The Santa Cruz Radio Observatory (ROSAC); the first radio astronomy facility in Costa Rica
Items.Abstract: The University of Costa Rica (UCR) is in the process of commissioning an 11-meter radio antenna as the initial infrastructure project for the newly created Santa Cruz Radio Observatory (ROSAC). Initially intended for solar monitoring in the frequency range 100KHz to 1GHz, the antenna could also operate as a teaching and research instrument for radioastronomy up to Ka band. Construction is being carried out with collaboration from Mexico´s National Astrophysics Institute. The antenna uses an 11-meter shaped primary reflector donated by the national telecommunications company, with an elevation-over-azimuth mount. We describe progress towards completion and operation, including the mechanical and optical system, construction, assembly, alignment and early testing. We discuss a simple primary-focus instrument for solar monitoring, and the plan for solar tracking. We provide an overview of financial, human and technical resources that have enabled the project to move forward since 2018.

Items.Authors: Federico Incardona, Alessandro Costa, Kevin Munari, Sebastiano Spinello, Emilio Mastriani, Igor Oya
Items.Title: The second release of the monitoring, logging, and alarm system for the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Monitoring, Logging, and Alarm System is the ACADA subsystem responsible for collecting operational monitoring values and logs, storing them for later inspection, and managing alarm events for the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory. This paper presents Release 2, focusing on updates to MON and AAS. The release introduces structured Java configuration models loaded through the ACADA Configuration Database REST API, replacing direct runtime interpretation of ICD Excel files for monitoring configuration. MON adds new interfaces for time-series data, metadata, recent values, FRAM events, and OB/SB state and phase histories. LOG improves deployment and runtime configuration of logshipper and logaggregator for adaptable log ingestion. AAS adds a REST API, an explicit alarm state machine, ACADA CDB-backed configuration, and complex alarm management based on the Integrated Alarm System (IAS).

Items.Authors: Yutaro Kasai, Hironobu Nakata, Shunsuke Adachi, Akito Kusaka, Osamu Tajima
Items.Title: The Simons Observatory: angle and relative gain calibration of the small-aperture telescopes using a sparse wire grid
Items.Abstract: The Simons Observatory aims to search for primordial gravitational waves through measurements of the polarization of the cosmic microwave background targeting a tensor-to-scalar ratio r of 0.003. To achieve this goal, it is essential to reduce systematic errors in the polarization angle and relative gain of the detectors. We have implemented an artificial polarized source, the Sparse Wire Grid, for calibration purposes. We will describe the analysis procedures and show the results.

Items.Authors: Yoshinori Sueno
Items.Title: The Simons Observatory: characterization of temperature-to-polarization leakage of small aperture telescopes
Items.Abstract: The Simons Observatory is a cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiment in the Atacama Desert in Chile, consisting of one Large Aperture Telescope and an array of Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs). A primary science goal of the SATs is to search for B-mode polarization that is predicted by inflationary models of the early universe. To achieve our target level, \sigma(r) = 0.003, controlling systematic effects is essential. Temperature-to-Polarization (T-to-P) leakage is particularly problematic, as the CMB temperature anisotropy is much larger than the B-mode signal. The continuously rotating half-wave plate employed by the SATs is expected to reduce the T-to-P leakage sources found in beam differencing experiments. We present the characterization of T-to-P leakage for the SATs using Jupiter observations. We describe the methodology and results that enable characterization at the O(0.01%) level, and discuss the impact of this leakage on the B-mode power spectrum.

Items.Authors: Ludovico Bizzarri
Items.Title: The Simons Observatory: characterization of the POLOCALC drone-borne calibration source
Items.Abstract: We characterize the POLOCALC drone-borne W-band source developed to calibrate state-of-the-art CMB telescopes. Laboratory measurements of RF components are used to predict the measured power by SO SATs. We estimate the efficiency of different SAT wafers across multiple W-band frequencies, by combining the power predictions with the actual power measured by the telescopes. The resulting efficiencies are consistent with independent calibration from planetary observations.

Items.Authors: Claire Lessler, Thomas Alford, Shreya Sutariya, Alex Thomas, Erin Healy, Jeff McMahon
Items.Title: The Simons Observatory: design and simulation of a bandpass calibration system for the Large Aperture Telescope
Items.Abstract: Mm-wave observations of the sky require precisely calibrated detector bandpasses to separate the astrophysical signals of the Cosmic Microwave Background, galactic foregrounds, and extragalactic sources. In the past year, the Simons Observatory (SO) has begun its wide-field, arcminute-resolution survey from Chile. Maximizing the science return from this survey motivates band-pass calibration accuracy approaching a tenth-of-a-percent for band centers. However, current state-of-the-art measurements using fourier transform spectrometers (FTSs) are limited by systematics at the few percent level. To address these systematics, we present the design of a robotically-controlled FTS system incorporating reflective coupling optics capable of making in-situ bandpass measurements to sub-percent uncertainty. We plan to use this system to make in-situ bandpass measurements of the SO Large-Aperture Telescope receiver, enabling the next generation of component-separated mm-wave maps of the sky.

Items.Authors: Junya Suzuki
Items.Title: The Simons Observatory: development of a new small-aperture telescope receiver for 30/40 GHz observations
Items.Abstract: The Simons Observatory operates multiple CMB telescopes in the Atacama Desert, with new small-aperture telescopes planned to improve sensitivity to primordial gravitational waves. The low-frequency SAT (SAT-LF), observing at 30 and 40 GHz, will enhance synchrotron foreground characterization for B-mode searches. Scheduled for deployment in 2027, SAT-LF includes over 1,600 TES detectors, a daisy-chained microwave readout system, and improved cryogenic and mechanical designs. This poster presents the current development status and key technical advancements.

Items.Authors: Yudai Seino
Items.Title: The Simons Observatory: gain and time-constant calibration stimulator for the Large Aperture Telescope
Items.Abstract: The Simons Observatory Large Aperture Telescope (LAT) uses over 60,000 Transition Edge Sensors to measure the Cosmic Microwave Background with high sensitivity. Frequent and accurate calibration of all detectors is essential for achieving its scientific goals. The LAT employs a stimulator that illuminates the receiver with modulated blackbody radiation, enabling simultaneous relative gain and time-constant calibration of the entire focal plane of detectors. This summary introduces the stimulator’s design, calibration approach, and initial results demonstrating its effectiveness for LAT operations.

Items.Authors: Thomas P. Satterthwaite
Items.Title: The Simons Observatory: initial characterization of the detector readout system for the enhanced large-aperture telescope
Items.Abstract: This contribution presents a characterization of the detector readout system for the Simons Observatory, a cosmic microwave background research facility located at 5,200 m in Chile’s Atacama Desert. The observatory consists of four telescopes: one 6 m large-aperture telescope (LAT) which aims to characterize a number of probes of the growth of large-scale structure, and an array of 0.42 m small-aperture telescopes which aim to constrain the energy scale of cosmic inflation. The LAT was recently upgraded by deploying an additional 32,000 detectors to its cryogenic receiver in early 2026. This upgrade will effectively double the telescope’s mapping speed, allowing it to reach a goal map depth of 2.6 μK-arcmin across 60% of the sky by the mid-2030s. This poster will report on an initial characterization of the microwave SQUID multiplexing readout system for the enhanced telescope's detectors.

Items.Authors: Hrushikesha Athreya, Zeeshan Ahme, Jay Austermann, Kyuyoung Bae, Aneesh Bapat, Darcy Barron, Pete Barry, Amy Bender, Bradford Benson, Lindsey Bleem, John Carlstrom, Tom Cecil, Clarence Chang, Stephen Cisneros, Anna Coerver, James Cornelison, Rahul Datta, Karia Dibert, Wilber Dominguez, Shannon Duff, Kyra Fichman, Jeff Fillipini, Pato Gallardo, Lisa Gades, Silvia Galli, Nils Halverson, Qing Hao, Shawn Henderson, William Holzapfel, Alec Hryciuk, Johannes Hubmayr, Dante Jones, Varun Kabra, Kirit Karkare, Cesiley King, Matthew Koc, Anna Kofman, Richard Lew, Michael Link, Tammy Lucas, Aashrita Mangu, Emily Martsen, Jeffrey McMahon, Joshua Montgomery, Johanna Nagy, Tyler Natoli, Hogan Nguyen, Val Novosad, Stephen Padin, Tristan Pinsonneault-Marotte, Srini Raghunathan, Alexandra Rahlin, Christian Reichardt, Larry Ruckman, John Ruhl, Shaaf Sarwar, Sara Simon, Robinjeet Singh, Joshua Sobrin, Antony Stark, Quinn Taylor, Carole Tucker, Joel Ullom, Jeffrey Van Lanen, Joaquin Vieira, Abigail Vieregg, Michael Vissers, Gensheng Wang, Kimmy Wu, Vlad Yefremenko, Elif Yilmaz, Cyndia Yu, Jeffrey Zivick, Ryan Herbst
Items.Title: The SPT-3G+ cryostat and optics tube design
Items.Abstract: I will present the mechanical and cryogenics design of the SPT-3G+ cryostat and camera optics, the next receiver planned to be installed on the South Pole Telescope. The system contains 14 detector arrays, each consisting of 90/150 GHz dichroic polarization-sensitive pixels, totaling 24,080 transition edge sensors (TES). Each detector array lies at the end of an optics tube, which are arranged in a hexagonal close-packed configuration to achieve a 4-deg diameter field of view. The optics and detectors are cooled by a combination of a pulse tube cooler for the 40K and 4K stages, and a dilution refrigerator for the 1K and 100 mK stages. Fabrication for the cryostat is aimed to start in 2026, with installation on SPT scheduled for the end of 2028, ahead of the 2029 winter observing season.

Items.Authors: Connor J. Langford, Peter Tuthill, Donald G. Dansereau, Christopher Betters, Karel Valenta, Brendan Cooper, Thomas Holland, George Ayad, Andrew Fleming
Items.Title: The TOLIMAN tip-tilt system: high accuracy pointing and stabilisation for astrometry onboard a CubeSat
Items.Abstract: The TOLIMAN mission aims to detect rocky, habitable-zone planets around nearby binary star systems using a 125mm diameter telescope onboard a 16U spacecraft in low Earth orbit. Achieving the mission’s science goals requires pointing accuracy better than 2 arcseconds and pointing stability below 1 arcsecond per second. This work presents the design of a novel fine-pointing system to meet these strict pointing requirements. The system will utilise piezo actuators to stabilise and correct the pointing of the telescope throughout imaging.

Items.Authors: D. Gale, S. Kurtz, F. Diaz, E. Colorado, D. Hiriart, T. Calvario, J. Cuazoson, D. Guerrero
Items.Title: The Tulancingo radio observatory in Mexico: project overview, challenges, and current status
Items.Abstract: In this paper we look back at the challenges and achievements of the Tulancingo telecommunications antenna conversion project, both the complex nature of ownership, stewardship and funding of science in Mexico, and the technical achievements, from antenna selection and feasibility study, through maintenance, upgrade and conversion activities , and finally software testing and early pointing and tracking results. We discuss the involvement of project stakeholders, and efforts to secure funding for conversion and operation, both nationally and through international programs. We also discuss the level of interest from local educational institutions and the public in general. Finally, the paper considers the role and value of an antenna conversion project in Mexico, where resources for science are limited and largely focused on established national priorities.

Items.Authors: Yu-Ting Wu, Ignacio Toledo, Hugo Messias, Celia Verdugo, Adele Plunket, Akiko Kawamura, Jorge Morgado, Hannah Stacey, Loreto Barcos-Muñoz
Items.Title: The use of the phase 2 tracking system to reduce observing failure rate
Items.Abstract: After the ALMA proposals are accepted, they transition into the Phase 2 Generation (P2G) stage. During this stage, the P2G group will review all proposals and ensure that the technical setup of the associated Scheduling Blocks (SBs) are compatible with ALMA's capabilities. To help the P2G group review the SBs and thus reducing observing failure rates, a Phase 2 Tracking System in the AI platform Dataiku was developed by the Taiwan ARC node with the help from the VISTA (Visualizations and Insights for ScienTific operations and Analytics) group and the Phase 2 Lead in ALMA. After analyzing the failure cases over three years, we show that the Phase 2 tracking system can reduce observing failure rates by a factor of ~1.7. We conclude the deployment of the Phase 2 tracking system will be essential to increase the observing efficiency, and should be included at the beginning of system-wide designs for projects.

Items.Authors: Gaston Gausachs, Tony Travouillon, Roland Bacon, Philippe Dierickx, Corentin Cudennec, David Lee, Jan Kragt, Ciro Del Vecchio, Simone D'Auria, Vincenzo De Caprio, Vincenzo Cianniello
Items.Title: The Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST): telescope structure and enclosure design challenges
Items.Abstract: The Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST) is a future 12-m class, alt-az optical telescope proposed for construction in Chile, near the European Southern Observatory (ESO) Cerro Paranal and Cerro Armazones installations. WST is capable of simultaneous observations in the visible through a Multi-Object Spectrograph (MOS) and Integral Field Spectrograph (IFS), collecting light at a common focal plane. The design, of both the telescope structure and the enclosure, captures the complexity of relaying the IFS beam to the numerous spectrographs at the base of the building and guiding the MOS fibres to the large spectrographs on the observing floor. This paper presents a detailed view into the different design challenges specific to those major systems. Early static and dynamic loadings are evaluated for different areas of the telescope using a combination of Finite Element Analyses (FEA) and Computer Fluid Dynamics (CFD).

Items.Authors: Daiki Morimoto, Yuichiro Ezoe, Kumi Ishikawa, Masaki Numazawa, Aoi Ishimure, Yuto Ogasawara, Syunei Miyauchi, Naoya Sera, Yu Fukushima, Masato Takeuchi, Daiki Ishi
Items.Title: Thermal cycle tests of MEMS X-ray optics for the GEO-X mission
Items.Abstract: We report on thermal tests of ultralight silicon X-ray optics using micromachining technologies for the GEO-X mission. It is a Wolter type-I optics made from two 300 µm-thick silicon substrates with micro-pores. Thermal cycle tests are conducted following to JAXA spacecraft general test standards : eight cycles between −5 degree C and 45 degree C with a rate of 1 degree C/min. Using ray-tracing simulations, we quantitatively defined requirements on potential deformation of the substrates after thermal cycles. Initial tests showed deformation of the substrates. Then we improved the design and the adhesion method of the substrates to a holder. After these improvements, the degradation after the thermal cycle test is significantly suppressed to meet requirements on the deformation.

Items.Authors: Ana Carolina Keiman Freire, Alejandro Farah Simon, Valente Vázquez-Velázquez, Rubén A. Flores-Meza, Fernando Ángeles , Joel Sánchez-Bermudez
Items.Title: Thermal modeling of a mount for securing the new germanium grism for the GRAVITY+ SUPER HIGH-RES
Items.Abstract: GRAVITY+ 1 will extend the capabilities of the GRAVITY instrument at the VLTI by improving sensitivity, astrometric precision, and spectral resolution. The SUPER HIGH-RES mode requires integration of a germanium (Ge) grism in a cryogenic opto-mechanical environment. This work presents a preliminary thermal analysis of the grism mount prior to experimental validation in COLIBRI and FCTF. Three geometrically identical mounts made of aluminum 5083, aluminum 6061, and PLA are evaluated using transient thermal simulations in ANSYS Workbench for 60 s and 600 s under conduction-dominated, cryogenic boundary conditions. Results show superior thermal uniformity for aluminum alloys, with aluminum 6061 exhibiting the lowest thermal gradients, while PLA performs significantly worse. These results support future thermo-mechanical modeling of the full assembly.

Items.Authors: Jonas W. Muegge, Valeria Antonelli, Marcus Maeder, Norbert Meidinger, Kirpal Nandra, Anirudh Saraf, Rafael Strecker, Steffen Marburg
Items.Title: Thermo-mechanical design trade-off for an x-ray detector module
Items.Abstract: The SPICE X-ray detector module requires a thermal isolation structure to separate the cold sensor and warm readout electronics. As 1000 wirebonds still cross the gap, this thermal isolation must also display a very high stiffness to limit damage to the sensor and wirebonds. Five different module concepts based on different materials and geometries are explained, then designed and simulated against one another to see which has the optimal thermal and vibrational performance. Test results from the final chosen design are discussed.

Items.Authors: Nicolás A. Rodríguez-Linares, José M. González-Cava, Luzma Montoya, Juan Albino Méndez Pérez, Yolanda Martín Hernando, M. Núñez-Cagigal
Items.Title: Tomographic reconstructors for MCAO: a solar case study
Items.Abstract: The European Solar Telescope (EST) will use a Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics (MCAO) system to obtain high spatial resolution solar images over a wide 60″ field of view. This system employs several deformable mirrors working together to correct the effects of atmospheric turbulence at different heights. Traditionally, solar telescopes rely on simple mathematical methods to combine the measurements from multiple sensors, mainly because more advanced techniques require higher computational power.  In this work, we explore modern tomographic reconstruction methods that can improve image quality and stability, comparing them with the classical approach currently used in existing solar MCAO systems. The analysis is carried out with SAOS, a new solar adaptive optics simulator developed within the EST project.

Items.Authors: Ahmad W. Sukkar, Ammar Abdulla, Ghena Rusheidat, Sara Al Nashar, Mariam Al Kaabi, Noor Alamm, Eslam Nofal, Mashhoor Al Wardat, Zouhair Benkhaldoun, Mohamed Gibril, Awni Khasawneh, Hamid Al Naimiy
Items.Title: Towards a pioneering, fully documented architectural design concept for an astronomical observatory in the UAE
Items.Abstract: This paper presents the preliminary architectural design framework and site assessment strategies for the development of an Astronomical Observatory in Sharjah, United Arab Emirates. The study integrates architectural design principles with environmental, scientific, and infrastructural considerations across two candidate locations. An interdisciplinary methodology combining architectural engineering, astronomy, environmental studies, and geospatial site evaluation was applied to analyze topography, accessibility, atmospheric conditions, vegetation distribution, and land-use constraints. The proposed design aims to balance functional requirements for optical & radio astronomical research with sustainable architectural solutions that respect the natural landscape. The outcomes demonstrate the role of collaborative processes in shaping astronomy infrastructure and establish the foundation for a fully developed observatory masterplan to support research, education, and public engagement i

Items.Authors: Matteo Simioni, Luca Cortese, Roland Wagner, Carmelo Arcidiacono, Andrea Grazian, Marco Gullieuszik, Elena Masciadri, Elisa Portaluri, Benedetta Vulcani, Anita Zanella, Richard Davies, Johanna Hartke, Roberto Piazzesi, Stefan Raffetseder, Piero Vaccari
Items.Title: Towards first light for MICADO: validation of the PSF-R service with real data
Items.Abstract: MICADO, one of the ELT’s first-light instruments, will rely on point-spread-function reconstruction (PSF-R) to meet scientific requirements, especially for SCAO observations of targets that lack bright reference stars nearby. PSF-R will be performed in post-processing using only AO telemetry, recorded simultaneously with the science data. During the initial SCAO phase, both on- and off-axis PSFs will be delivered. We present the current status and results from an ESO TTR campaign begun in 2023, targeting a sparse three-star asterism under varied conditions with the ERIS instrument at VLT. Reconstructed PSFs reach ~10% accuracy in Strehl ratio and FWHM at separations up to 16″.

Items.Authors: Manon Lallement, Louis Gemmerlé, Pierre R. Labeye, Jean-Philippe Berger, Guillermo Martin, Stéphane Curaba, Rémi Armand
Items.Title: Towards integrated mid-infrared nulling interferometry: characterization of SiGe-on-Si photonic integrated circuits on the MILENE optical bench
Items.Abstract: Nulling interferometry suppresses on-axis starlight through destructive interference, enabling exoplanet detection and characterization. Traditional bulk-optics nullers can be voluminous, whereas Photonic Integrated Circuits (PIC) provide a compact and thermo-mechanically stable alternative, enabling complex light routing. While most PIC efforts have targeted the near-infrared, extending their capabilities to the mid-infrared is both challenging and essential, as this region hosts key molecular signatures that the NOTT instrument and the LIFE mission aim to investigate. We present the characterization of mid-infrared PIC for nulling interferometry performed at IPAG on the MILENE bench. The devices, fabricated at CEA-LETI using the SiGe-on-Si technology, are optimized for 3-5 µm operation with possible extension to 11 µm. We report performance of 2- and 4-telescope PIC, including spectral coverage, transmission, and null depth, and show initial results on active thermal phase control.

Items.Authors: Gavin Frueh, J. Goodman, Hanyuan Liang, Kenneth Buffo, Paul Reid, Susan Trolier-McKinstry, Thomas N. Jackson, Casey T. DeRoo
Items.Title: Towards realizing adjustable X-ray optics for astronomy using TFT-addressed thin-film PZT actuators
Items.Abstract: We report on progress towards realizing adjustable X-ray optics with thin-film actuators. These mirror devices utilize thin-film lead zirconate titanate (PZT) as a piezoelectric actuator, with ZnO thin-film transistors (TFTs) to allow simple array addressing. By dividing this film into discrete cells and applying a low voltage, the actuators produce a localized, biaxial strain. Manufacturing thin-film actuator stacks and TFTs on the non-reflective sides of thin segments is hence a viable technology pathway for realizing high performance X-ray optics. In this presentation, we discuss the requirements for and benefits of adapting from glass to silicon mirror substrates. Furthermore, we report on measurements of the thin-film stresses associated with stages of device fabrication process as measured via interferometry, and discuss the progress towards compensating for the net integrated stress with controlled growth of a silicon dioxide layer.

Items.Authors: Gaspar Fábrega, Pedro P. Silva, Ingeborg A. Muñoz, Juan P. Gil, Eduardo Peña
Items.Title: Transitional on-premises data platform: preparing Paranal Observatory infrastructure for hybrid cloud operations
Items.Abstract: The evolution of Paranal Observatory’s data-centric paradigm requires a careful transition to avoid disrupting operations. We describe the implementation of a transitional data platform that updates current on-premise infrastructure to modern containerized standards while preserving essential functionality. Leveraging Kubernetes, ArgoCD, GitLab CI/CD, and Vault, this intermediate platform serves two purposes: improving current operations while testing the technologies and practices necessary for future hybrid cloud deployment. The platform addresses critical requirements including upgrade processes, security, and reproducible deployment through GitOps methodologies. Migration strategies ensure continuity of monitoring capabilities while progressively incorporating cloud-native patterns. The resulting infrastructure represents a path forward that balances innovation with operational stability.

Items.Authors: Kathryn Hartley, James Osborn, David Alaluf, Alejandro Rodriguez, Adolfo Comeron, Perrine Lognone, Lai Zhang, Ryan Griffiths, Lily Beesley
Items.Title: TURBO: a 24-hour turbulence monitoring facility in Barcelona
Items.Abstract: Atmospheric optical turbulence limits the performance of both astronomy and free-space optical communication links between the ground and space. In this talk we present TURBO - a turbulence monitoring facility, based on the 24-hour Shack-Hartmann Image Motion Monitor (24hSHIMM) instrument, capable of measuring optical atmospheric turbulence 24-hours a day. TURBO will be an autonomous turbulence monitor generating valuable data for both the FSOC and Astronomy community. In addition, we present TURBO 2,3 & 4 which are portable SHIMM instruments designed for running turbulence monitoring campaigns across Europe. These instruments can be used for site characterisation, cross validation with other turbulence profilers and for AO system tests and development. The results from this research facility will provide essential insights for optical ground station (OGS) site selection and future OGS design as well as vital data for training and testing turbulence forecasting models.

Items.Authors: Z. Song, X. Wei, J. Ge, Q. Hu, Zh. Sun, Y. Yang
Items.Title: Ultra-high precision fine guidance sensor design and simulation for the Earth 2.0 (ET) Space mission
Items.Abstract: The Earth 2.0 (ET) space mission uses space-based wide-field ultra-high precision photometry for exoplanet transit surveys, addressing fundamental questions like terrestrial planet formation and the search for extraterrestrial life. Its Fine Guidance Sensor (FGS) is the core for attitude control, enabling these observations. Targeting the ET mission's ten-milliarcsecond precision requirement, this paper presents an ultra-high precision FGS design integrating star detection, boresight attitude calculation, and acquisition. Key technologies such as high-precision star centroid estimation and robust star identification are analyzed and modeled. A multi-source collaborative adaptive guide star parameter adjustment fusion algorithm is proposed. A semi-physical closed-loop simulation from MATLAB to FPGA is constructed. Results show boresight attitude error (1σ) ≤15 mas, surpassing Euclid's 25 mas, demonstrating capability to meet ET's stringent stability requirements.

Items.Authors: Timothy E. Pickering, Lisa Crause, Encarni Romero Colmenero, Rudi Kuhn, Nico van der Merwe
Items.Title: Upgraded seeing monitor for the South African Astronomical Observatory
Items.Abstract: Automated measurement of atmospheric seeing began at the South African Astronomical Observatory (SAAO) in March 2010. The original equipment consisted of a MASS-DIMM mated to a 25 cm Meade LX200 with the DIMM channel feeding a high-speed (200+ fps) IEEE1394 camera. That hardware eventually succumbed to the ravages of time. The interfaces to the MASS and DIMM camera because obsolete and difficult to support. The key failure, though, was that the mount could no longer point or track well enough to be useful anymore.    In 2024 the system was upgraded significantly and returned to routine operation. The DIMM camera and mount were replaced with newer, more performant options and the MASS-DIMM was replaced with a simple DIMM mask. We will present results from the first two years of renewed operation. These results will be compared to seeing measurements from other sources at the SAAO site. We will also describe the updated software the was developed for this system.

Items.Authors: Sang-Mok Cha, Chung-Uk Lee, Gregory Bredthauer, Ho Jin, Dong-Jin Kim, Seong-Cheol Bang, Seung-Lee Kim, Sungwook E. Hong
Items.Title: Upgrading the KMTNet 18k CCD cameras with Archon Electronics: laboratory validation and deployment plan
Items.Abstract: The Korea Microlensing Telescope Network (KMTNet) 18k CCD camera, using four CCD290-99 detectors, has shown limitations including tearing patterns, incomplete charge clearing, long-tail bleeding near bright sources, inter-channel crosstalk, overscan bias instability, and long readout overhead. To address these issues, we interfaced the existing engineering camera with an STA wallboard and Archon controller. Laboratory tests demonstrate complete removal of tearing, effective charge clearing without a flushing cycle, elimination of long-tail bleeding, and negligible crosstalk and overscan variations enabled by improved clocking and differential signal-processing electronics. Expanding the readout from 8 to 16 channels also reduced total readout time by half. These upgrades improve detector performance and are expected to enhance the scientific yield of future KMTNet observations. This presentation will describe the laboratory results and the deployment plan for the full camera upgrade.

Items.Authors: Benoît Neichel, Morgan Gray, Pierre Janin-Potiron, Giovanni Tramparulo, Arnaud Malvache, Vincent Chambouleyron, Jean-François Sauvage, Thierry Fusco
Items.Title: Using a network of smart telescopes to measure atmospheric turbulence
Items.Abstract: Atmospheric turbulence limits ground-based astronomy and optical communications, yet current monitoring remains sparse and costly. We propose using the global network of Unistellar smart telescopes as a distributed turbulence-sensing system. By extracting turbulence parameters from routine observations, each telescope becomes a local sensor, enabling a worldwide, high-cadence monitoring network. This approach provides users with real-time observing indicators and generates a large database to improve turbulence climatology, power ML-based predictions, and optical-communication infrastructure.

Items.Authors: Teresa Mineo, Davide Mollica, Ciro Bigongiari, Francesco G. Saturni, Fausto Casaburo, Giancarlo Cusumano
Items.Title: Using muon rings for the optical calibration of ASTRI Mini Array telescopes
Items.Abstract: The ASTRI Mini-Array, consisting of nine innovative Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes, is an INAF project dedicated to studying gamma-ray sources that emit at very high energies in the TeV range. It is located at the Teide Astronomical Observatory (Tenerife, Canary Islands), where seven of the nine telescopes have been installed. Two of them (ASTRI-1 and ASTRI-3) already acquire Cherenkov data, while the remaining units, currently under completion, are expected to be completed by the end of 2026.  The analysis of muon ring images, commonly detected by Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes during regular observations, is a standard technique used to calibrate the optical throughput and monitor the optical point spread function. It has been integrated into the ASTRI Mini-Array calibration plan as one of the key methods. In this contribution, we present results from the analysis of muon events collected by the two operating telescopes.

Items.Authors: Sarah E. Logsdon, Emily Hunting, Shubham Kanodia, Daniel Krolikowski, Arvind F. Gupta, William R. McBride, Jayadev Rajagopal, Chad F. Bender
Items.Title: Using On-sky, Signal-to-Noise Triggered Observations to Monitor Telescope Mirror Reflectivity Performance
Items.Abstract: This work explores the use of signal-to-noise (S/N) triggered observations for monitoring telescope mirror reflectivity performance over time. We analyze data obtained by the NEID spectrometer on the bare-aluminum coated, WIYN 3.5 m Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The NEID system includes a chromatic exposure meter that provides high-cadence flux monitoring and allows flexible, S/N based exposures. Here we present a comprehensive analysis of NEID S/N trigger data in fixed weather bins as a proxy for temporal mirror reflectivity measurements. We quantify the impact of a degrading coating in terms of hours of science time on sky and illustrate the potential efficiency gains for queue-based observing from informed mirror recoating schedules. We compare the S/N results to both traditional reflectometry measurements and system throughput measurements and discuss the advantages of an exposure meter for providing a science-driven metric for mirror recoating timescales.

Items.Authors: Till Hagelschuer, Dennis Wendler, Ingo Walter, Martin Pertenais, Matthias Lieder, Simone del Togno, Gisbert Peter, Andreas Pohl, Steffen Babben, Yaquelin Miriam Rosas Ortiz, Andrei Cacovean, Sergio Rufini Mastropasqua, Pascal Thabaut, Horst-Georg Lötzke, Karsten Westerdorff, Carlos Arcos Carrasco, Alexander Fitzner, Emanuel Kopp, Eitan Pechevis, Marion Bonafous, Jerome Parisot, Didier Zeganadin, Jean-Michel Reess, Tristan Buey, Giulia Alemanno, Ana-Catalina Plesa
Items.Title: VEM structural and thermal models development and testing for VERITAS and EnVision
Items.Abstract: We report on the VEM structural and thermal HW models developed for early testing of the instrument. Because of the challenging dynamic, shock load, temperature and sun illumination environment expected during the two Venus missions VERITAS and EnVision, this is of high importance, since any necessary design impact must be identified early to allow for adapting the flight model design. Three models are used for our investigations. An instrument structural model to check the dynamic and shock loads and to derive qualification loads for the subsystems. A Focal Plane Assembly Thermal Model to check the thermal behavior along the FPA chain. Finally, a flight-representative VEM baffle model for thermal qualification against sun illumination.    The test results reported shall confirm the current VEM design or provide design adjustments if needed, such that the engineering qualification model can be prepared for manufacturing. EQM qualification shall be done until summer 2027 before VEM CDR.

Items.Authors: R. De Cock, H.-P. Gröbelbauer, N. Eaton, S. Kögl, P. Bogaert, L. Jacobs, B. Beeckman, S. Berkenbosch, O. Döbrich, J. Erwin, S. Robert, P. Seiler, F. Wirz, S. Stutz, G. Székely, P. Kögl, A. Aubry, N. Pereira, D. Bolsée, P. Tackley, M. Ferus, P. Machado, M. Min, L. M. Lara, G. Alemanno, E. Marcq, O. Barraud, E. Neefs
Items.Title: VenSpec-H: a cold-box-in-warm-box proof of concept
Items.Abstract: VenSpec-H is an infrared spectrometer, part of the EnVision mission of ESA to planet Venus. The core optical part of the instrument needs to be cooled down to -45 °C with a maximum gradient of 2°C, while other parts must stay relatively warm (around -10 °C). This led to a design based on a so-called cold-box-in-warm-box concept with the cold box suspended on top of blade flexures inside the warm box.  The proof of this concept is shown here, reporting on the vibration and thermal-vacuum tests that have been performed on a representative breadboard model and the good correlation between the physical and the numerical models.

Items.Authors: Manuel Gomez-Jimenez, Craig Lage, Alex Broughton, Braulio Cancino, Rolando Cantarutti, Charles F. Claver, Patricio Cortes, Eric Coughlin, Sylvie Dagoret-Campagne, Erik Dennihy, Norman Diaz, Parker Fragelius, Robert H. Lupton, Marc Moniez, Fritz Mueller, Freddy Muñoz Arancibia, Jeremy Neveu, Eske M. Pedersen, Tiago Ribeiro, Mario Rivera, Martin Rodriguez-Monroy, Eli S. Rykoff, Alysha Shugart, Sandrine Thomas, Roberto Tighe, Elana K. Urbach, Wouter van Reeven
Items.Title: Vera C. Rubin’s auxiliary telescope ascent: fault mitigation and the transition from construction to reliable operations
Items.Abstract: The Vera C. Rubin’s Auxiliary Telescope (AuxTel) is a 1.2 m observatory equipped with the LATISS spectrograph, specifically designed to determine the atmospheric transmission above the observatory site in Chile. This function is essential to satisfy the photometric precision and accuracy requirements for the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). The AuxTel project was successfully completed, meeting all functional and cost specifications. The transition to operations focused heavily on executing a rigorous fault mitigation strategy, in close collaboration with other engineers within the different programs of NOIRLab, to stabilize the system’s core performance, increasing system reliability and maintainability. AuxTel is now in its operational phase, delivering the necessary atmospheric transmission data products, ensuring the long-term science mission of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Items.Authors: Robert Spry, Jake D. Hutchinson, Roy Preece, Adam D. Wilkinson, John-Paul Walker, Robert Watkins, Rebecca Holleb, Emma Ryan, Cédric Pereira, David Castro Alves, Fraser Clarke, Greg King, Waqas Mir, Manuel Abreu, Neil Bowles
Items.Title: Verification methods for the Ariel optical ground support equipment
Items.Abstract: In this proceeding, we present the integration and verification plan for the Ariel Optical Ground Support Equipment (OGSE), showing how the different technical requirements will be verified. Ariel is a 1 m class cryogenic (∼ 40 K) telescope used to make spectroscopic measurements of ~1000 exoplanet atmospheres. The integrated payload will be tested at RAL Space using the OGSE.   To test the payload on the ground, the OGSE needs to meet very stringent performance requirements. Notable examples include: the 214nm RMS wavefront flatness at a 70K operational temperature, 24ppm detector photometric stability on hour timescales, radiometric calibration with 5% relative accuracy, and a flat fielding capability with a uniformity better than 0.5%. In this proceeding, we will describe how the various performance and functional verifications will be achieved.

Items.Authors: Andrea Scaudo, Matteo Genoni, Marco Landoni, David Young, Paolo D'Avanzo, Sergio Campana, Pietro Schipani, Lorenzo Cabona, Matteo Aliverti, Gianluca Li Causi, José A. Araiza-Durán, Iair Arcavi, Andrea Baruffolo, Federico Battaini, Sagi Ben-Ami, Alex Bichkovsky, Anna Brucalassi, Giulio Capasso, Enrico Cappellaro, Riccardo Claudi, Mirko Colapietro, Rosario Cosentino, Francesco D'Alessio, Sergio D'Orsi, Massimo Della Valle, Simone Di Filippo, Avishay Gal-Yam, Ofir Hershko, Hanindyo Kuncarayakti, Luigi Lessio, Laurent Marty, Seppo Mattila, Matteo Munari, Giuliano Pignata, Kalyan Radhakrishnan, Michael Rappaport, Davide Ricci, Marco Riva, Adam Rubin, Bernardo Salasnich, Salvatore Savarese, Salvatore Scuderi, Stephen Smartt, Maximilian Stritzinger, Fabrizio Vitali, Ricardo Zanmar Sanchez, Emanuela Pompei
Items.Title: Verification of the SOXS Exposure Time Calculator from the instrument commissioning at the ESO-NTT
Items.Abstract: We present the updated Exposure Time Calculator (ETC) for SOXS, a single-object spectrograph at the ESO 3.58 m New Technology Telescope (NTT). SOXS combines UV–VIS and NIR arms to cover 350–2000 nm with a mean resolving power of about 4500. The Python-based, web-accessible ETC predicts signal-to-noise ratios and exposure times as a function of target properties, atmospheric conditions, and instrumental setup, and provides additional outputs such as expected count rates and detailed noise contributions. We outline the revised architecture and main observing modes, and show how ETC predictions are used to quantify and monitor SOXS performance by comparison with commissioning measurements at La Silla.

Items.Authors: María Eugenia Redondo González, Sebastiaan Haffert, Warren B. Foster, Jared R. Males, Olivier Guyon, Laird M. Close, Roswell Roberts, Elena Tonucci, Kyle van Gorkom, Alexander Hedglen, Parker T. Johnson, Maggie Y. Kautz, Jay K. Kueny, Jialin Li, Joshua Liberman, Joseph D. Long, Jennifer Lumbres, Matthijs Mars, Eden A. McEwen, Avalon McLeod, Logan A. Pearce, Lauren Schatz, Katie Twitchell
Items.Title: Visible light spectroscopy with extreme adaptive optics: a pipeline for the low-resolution mode of VIS-X
Items.Abstract: We present a data reduction pipeline for the low-resolution mode of VIS-X, the integral-field spectrograph of extreme adaptive optics system MagAO-X, at the Magellan Clay telescope. The pipeline reconstructs calibrated spectral data cubes over 450-900 nm, extracting spectra from the detector for a hundred wavelength channels. On-sky observations of spectroscopic binary 42 Ori demonstrate the pipeline’s potential to disentangle individual spectra. Such capabilities will be essential for future extreme adaptive optics systems targeting the characterisation of companions’ atmospheres in the visible.

Items.Authors: Celia Verdugo, Ignacio Toledo, Adele Plunket, Jorge Morgado, Hannah Stacey, Akiko Kawamura, Yu-Ting Wu
Items.Title: Visualizations and insights for ScienTific operations and analytics for ALMA
Items.Abstract: The Joint ALMA Observatory launched a Data Science Initiative in 2023 to foster evidence-based decision making. The VISTA (Visualizations and Insights for ScienTific operations and Analytics) group was created to standardize and automate reports for analytics. VISTA acts as a Data Steward, providing curated data for self-service reporting to science groups and the Proposal Handling Team. They ensure data quality by liaising with regional centers. Using Dataiku, VISTA has delivered insights for ALMA proposal statistics and contact scientist tracking tools. They also migrated vital data acquisition reports from a software subsystem to the new data science platform, allowing greater flexibility and visual insights. These data-centric efforts have been highly valued and demonstrate the team's significant potential

Items.Authors: Kelian Sommer, Brock A. Parker, Stephen Kaye, Aafaque R. Khan, Erika Hamden
Items.Title: VUV-to-VIS quantum efficiency measurements of Skipper CCDs detectors
Items.Abstract: We present a VUV-to-visible (150–650 nm) quantum-efficiency (QE) characterization system developed to evaluate low-noise Skipper CCDs for astronomical applications. The setup —featuring stabilized light sources, a vacuum monochromator, and calibrated photodiode standards— enables accurate QE and photon-transfer measurements in the challenging vacuum-UV regime. We report QE results for two OSCURA Skipper CCDs tested with both the Fermilab’s Low Threshold Acquisition (LTA) and STA’s Archon controllers, finding strong agreement with prior independent measurements. These results demonstrate a reliable pathway for systematic QE characterization of future UV-optimized Skipper CCDs intended for faint-signal astronomy.

Items.Authors: Helawae Kelemu, Alejandro Buendía, Deborah Malone, Saúl Perez, Francisco Javier De Cos Juez, Nazim Ali Bharmal, Tim Morris
Items.Title: Wavefront predictor performance comparison between artificial neural network and linear model-based predictors
Items.Abstract: Modern astronomical telescopes employ high-dimensional adaptive optics (AO) systems. In such systems, wavefront prediction is essential for mitigating temporal-lag errors. Neural network–based predictors have seen increased interest, yet direct comparisons with linear model-based predictors remain scarce.  This work presents a comparative evaluation of a linear predictor in an LQG control framework and a 2D-LSTM neural network predictor. Under non-stationary turbulence, the two approaches show distinct performance characteristics, with the neural network exhibiting greater adaptability. These findings support the development of self-calibrating model-based prediction strategies for future AO systems.

Items.Authors: Andrew W. Serio, Sharon E. Hunt, Josie Fenske, Hernan Chacana, Carolina Vargas
Items.Title: What does it mean? Introduction to NOIRLab’s terminology extension
Items.Abstract: NSF NOIRLab, which is funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), was formed in 2019 by consolidating three observatories (NOAO, International Gemini Observatory, and NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory). As a result, the organization inherited multiple disparate terminology databases from its Programs, leading to confusion and duplication of effort regarding the meaning and usage of terms and abbreviations. We have consolidated these terminology sources into a single, authoritative database that includes terms and abbreviations for common astronomical language, job titles, Program-specific items, organizations and institutions, and instrumentation, with both English and Spanish translations to support our multilingual, international organization. The database powers the NOIRLab Terminology Extension, a Chrome extension that provides an easy search feature overlayable on any web page. Users can find the expanded forms of acronyms and see term usage differences across NOIRLab.

Items.Authors: Nicholas B. Galitzki
Items.Title: The Simons Observatory: commissioning and initial science observations
Items.Abstract: The Simons Observatory (SO) measures the cosmic microwave background (CMB) from a high altitude (5,200 m) site in Chile’s Atacama Desert. SO makes precision temperature and polarization maps on angular scales between one arcminute and tens of degrees using over 120,000 detectors operating below 100 mK and sampling frequencies between 24 and 315 GHz. SO consists of one six-meter-aperture telescope and an array of half-meter aperture refractive cameras with a photovoltaic system designed to supply 70% of the observatory’s energy needs. The observatory is fully operational and work on initial science publications and data products is advancing rapidly. We present the status of the observatory, covering the current configuration’s commissioning, operations, and initial observations as well as progress towards expanded capabilities.

Items.Authors: Carole G. Mundell
Items.Title: Driving cosmic discovery science at the frontiers of engineering and technology innovation
Items.Abstract: The European Space Agency Space Science programme aims to answer fundamental questions about the nature of the Universe and our place in it. To do so, it is vital to invent and implement novel technologies, materials, production processes and inflight operations - all within a financially constrained programme and design-to-cost model. The ESA Space Science programme brings together 23 ESA member states, drives new capabilities in European industry and underpins international collaborations beyond Europe. Prof Mundell will share ground-breaking scientific discoveries enabled by breakthrough technologies as the Cosmic Vision missions are delivered over the coming years, and - through the new ESA Voyage 2050 strategy - will give a look to the future of Europe in the global context of space science, astrophysics, heliophysics, planetary science, and exploration.

Items.Authors: Jifeng Liu
Items.Title: Building the future of astronomy: China’s astronomical infrastructure and the next 10-Year roadmap
Items.Abstract: Over the past decade, China has made substantial progress in building world-class astronomical facilities. Flagship infrastructures such as the LAMOST, FAST, EP, and SVOM have significantly strengthened our capabilities in optical, radio and high-energy time-domain astronomy. Looking ahead, we are planning a new generation of facilities including CSST, GOTTA, FASTA, a 14.5-meter optical telescope, a 120-meter-class radio telescope, and a strategic program focused on the origins of cosmic structures. Our roadmap emphasizes three major directions: expanding time-domain monitoring toward high cadence and multi-band all-sky coverage; advancing ultra-deep observations of faint and distant objects; and accelerating the development of space-based astronomy, while fostering international partnerships and promoting open-science frameworks that enable broader global participation. This talk will present recent achievements and outline China’s vision for the next 10 years of astronomical infrastructure, scientific discovery, and global collaboration.

Items.Authors: Javier León Gil, Antonio Zamora-Jiménez, Ángel Mato, Nicolás Rodríguez-Linares, Juan Cózar-Castellano, Miguel Núñez-Cagigal, Mary Barreto, José Manuel González Cava, Juan Albino Méndez Pérez
Items.Title: A design-phase approach to structural vibrations in ground-based telescopes: Application to the European Solar Telescope (EST)
Items.Abstract: The European Solar Telescope (EST), a 4-m class solar telescope equipped with a multi-conjugate adaptive optics system, will operate in an open-dome configuration, making it highly sensitive to wind-induced vibrations that degrade image stability. This paper presents a global strategy for vibration management to be applied from the earliest design phases of ground-based telescopes. The methodology defines criteria for allocating vibration levels across the structure and relies on modelling tools to assess their impact on image quality. It also introduces an optimization process that links image-stability requirements to image-motion specifications and frequency assignments. To evaluate the methodology, different vibration sources at various telescope locations are analysed, and the approach is applied to a simulation-based use case for the EST. Preliminary results and their implications for guiding key design decisions are also discussed.
